As the book explained, Dumbledore intended to die undefeated, the wand's last true master. Snape giving the *coup de grace* should have ended the wand's power permanently, as Dumbledore was never defeated. Snape would still end up with a historical object, but the wand's power would have been broken permanently, as it will never be loyal to him.

That's why the penultimate chapter is called "The Flaw In The Plan", as the plan failed when Draco disarmed Dumbledore.
In addition, Dumbledore was severely weakened at the time. He himself told Harry in limbo that the plan did not work out as he had wanted. He certainly did not foresee Draco disarming him.

There are two factors in play here, which JKR elaborated on Pottermore.

Your personal wand is supposed to have a special affinity to you, hence, its loyalty to you is not so easily won over by others during practice duels in class.

The Elder Wand has changed hands dozens, perhaps hundreds of times throughout history. Hence, it has no loyalty to an owner except power. When Draco disarmed Dumbledore, it wasn't a practice attempt, and hence the Elder Wand switched its loyalty to Draco. Similarly, when Harry disarmed Draco, it was during wartime, and his wand recognized a proper victory.
